why: Pass 1 enumerated 9 documents as the coverage denominator.

meta.audience: someone who just found the repo
Claude Code / Codex, at load time
an agent working out what its harness can do
whoever has to fix a red test
whoever wires ponder to a database

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The repository has no README at all
finding.detail: `ls README.md` fails. A visitor landing in ~/code/ponder gets a bare directory listing: bin, docs, install.sh, lenses, lib, oca, package.json, skill, SPEC.md, test. SPEC.md is the contract and reads like one — 377 lines opening on vocabulary tables — so the only entry point is a document written for implementers, not for someone deciding whether this tool is for them.
finding.recommendation: Write README.md as the front door: what ponder is, the problem it solves, install, the loop in one diagram, a 60-second quickstart, the command table, the convergence signals, OCA and how to turn it off, and where the lenses live.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: No document states the install story end to end
finding.detail: install.sh does the work and harness-notes.md explains the symlinks, but harness-notes lives three directories down inside the skill and is written for an agent reasoning about its own harness, not for a human installing the tool.
finding.recommendation: Put the install path in the README: run install.sh, what it symlinks into which harness, and how to verify with ponder doctor.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: SPEC 6.1 misstates the cognitive_events enum
finding.detail: SPEC.md:310 says of cognitive_event_type: "Only these existing labels may be used" and lists seven, adding "Never invent a label — the insert will fail." The live enum in postgres://localhost/oneiro has 33 labels; the seven are a subset. The restriction is a sound design choice, but it is stated as a fact about the database and that fact is wrong, which makes a reader distrust the surrounding table.
finding.recommendation: Reword as a deliberate restriction rather than a claim about the schema: "the enum carries more labels than these; ponder deliberately uses only this subset."

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: SPEC 3.4 never says whether pass-1 seeding is recorded as deltas
finding.detail: SPEC 3.4 fixes the delta vocabulary and the ledger rules but is silent on whether `ponder grade`'s pass-1 seeding lands on the ledger. SPEC 4 then divides add-deltas and total-deltas by total findings, so the silence decides novelty and churn on pass 1. The engine records the seed, which pins pass-1 novelty near 1.0; the conformance suite raises it as a warning rather than asserting either reading, because the contract does not settle it.
finding.recommendation: Add one sentence to SPEC 3.4 ruling on it, and say what pass-1 novelty and churn are expected to read as a consequence.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: SPEC 5.2's --severity wording is self-contradictory
finding.detail: SPEC.md:283 says apply selects findings "at or above --severity", which reads as a threshold, but the signature in the same section is `--severity must,should`, which reads as an explicit set. Both readings pass the current implementation, so nothing forces the ambiguity into the open.
finding.recommendation: Pick one. If it is a threshold, write `--severity must` and say the rest are implied; if it is a set, drop "at or above".

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: "Nothing in the engine locks anything" is false
finding.detail: The Known bites section states that nothing in the engine locks, and claims a reproduction where two concurrent `ponder delta` calls both succeed and the loser's edit is lost. The engine has held an advisory session lock since lib/session.js:369, every mutating command takes it via useSession(..., {lock: true}), and the conformance suite pins the opposite behaviour in 45 checks: a race has exactly one winner and the ledger grows by exactly one line. An agent reading this will architect around a hazard that no longer exists.
finding.recommendation: Replace the bite with what is now true: the engine takes an advisory lock per session, a race has one winner, and the guidance that only the parent runs ponder stands for a different reason — fan-out agents grade and return text.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Machine-specific facts are stated without a shelf life
finding.detail: The document opens "Facts below were verified on Quinn's personal Mac on 2026-08-24: node v25.5.0 and psql at /opt/homebrew/bin, codex-cli 0.147.0", then mixes those with durable architectural facts. A reader cannot tell which lines expire.
finding.recommendation: Split the machine-specific block into its own section headed with the verification date, and leave the architectural claims undated.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The status document contradicts itself on where it lives
finding.detail: The file opens with a banner saying it belongs in the Obsidian vault and could not be written there because macOS TCC denies access, with a cp command to run after granting Full Disk Access. So the copy in the repo is by its own account not the real one, and there is no way to tell whether the vault copy now exists and has diverged.
finding.recommendation: Either make the repo copy canonical and delete the banner, or move it and leave a one-line pointer. Two copies with a banner explaining why is the worst of the three.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Open threads have gone stale
finding.detail: "No real-world session run yet against a live project of Quinn's" is listed as an open thread, and the log records Phase 1 as complete with six lens packs built. The repo now carries a worked session under docs/example-session/, so the first thread is answered and nothing in the document points at it.
finding.recommendation: Close the thread and link the example session, or the document stops being a status and becomes a snapshot.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: protocol.md restates SPEC.md and will drift from it
finding.detail: protocol.md is a 441-line mirror of the contract — state layout, phase machine, every command, every file shape, the convergence table and the verdict rules. It names SPEC.md as the authority and says SPEC.md wins on disagreement, which is the right disclaimer, but a disclaimer does not stop drift: two documents now have to be edited together on every contract change and nothing checks that they were.
finding.recommendation: Cut the sections that only restate SPEC (convergence signals, verdict rules) down to a pointer, and keep protocol.md for what SPEC deliberately does not carry: worked JSON payloads and the error catalogue.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The prompts cite a path no reader outside this machine can open
finding.detail: The document says the prompts are adapted from the real engine at ~/oneiro/oca-cognitive/deliberation/engine.js and quotes each OCA system prompt verbatim. The quotes carry their own weight, but the citation is unresolvable for anyone who is not on Quinn's Mac, and it is the only evidence offered that the two systems match.
finding.recommendation: Keep the verbatim quotes, mark the path as a local source, and note the OCA version or date they were taken from.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: SKILL.md hard-codes an absolute path to the binary
finding.detail: The opening tells the agent "The binary is ~/code/ponder/bin/ponder (symlink it to ~/.local/bin/ponder, which is on PATH, or call the absolute path)." That is true on this machine and false on any other checkout, and it is in the first screen an agent reads.
finding.recommendation: Lead with `ponder` on PATH, and give the repo-relative fallback rather than one user's home directory.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The test count is written into prose and goes stale on every added test
finding.detail: "A full run is 64 tests in about three minutes" is a number a reader will trust and a number that changes whenever anyone adds a test. It had already drifted once.
finding.recommendation: Say "about sixty tests in roughly three minutes", or drop the count and keep the runtime.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The bridge README documents writes far better than reads
finding.detail: Every table ponder writes gets a column-by-column section and a set of runnable SQL recipes for reading a session back out. The two reads the engine actually performs — priorPondering at start and openObservations at judge — are covered mostly from the writer's side, and openObservations only appears in the degradation table.
finding.recommendation: Give the two reads a short section of their own: the query, when it fires, and what the engine does with the result.

why: Every seeded finding grades one document in isolation, so a gap in the shape of the set as a whole could not appear as one of them.

finding.title: No document shows a complete session from start to converged stop
finding.detail: SPEC.md defines the phases, protocol.md documents each command's payload, and SKILL.md carries a worked example written as instructions to an agent. None of them is a real session: there is no ledger a reader can open, no metrics.json to see the signals move, no report.md to see what the output actually looks like. A reader has to assemble the loop in their head from three documents before they can judge whether it is worth running.
finding.recommendation: Commit one real session to the repo and link it from the README, so the ledger, the metrics and the report can be read rather than described.

why: Zero dependencies is the most unusual property this tool has, and no pass had asked where a reader would find it stated.

finding.title: The zero-dependency guarantee is buried in a numbered non-negotiable
finding.detail: SPEC 8.5 says 'Zero npm dependencies. Node's standard library and psql only.' That is a headline property — it is why this can be symlinked into two harnesses and run anywhere node is — and it appears once, as item 5 of a list at the very bottom of a 377-line contract.
finding.recommendation: State it wherever a reader first meets the tool, not only where the contract enumerates its constraints.

why: The recommendation ended on a judgment about what the document becomes rather than a change somebody can make.

set.recommendation: Delete the 'No real-world session run yet' bullet, and replace it with a link to docs/example-session/ naming the subject, the pass count and the stop reason.

why: An unresolvable path is the first thing that breaks for an agent on another machine, which is the audience a skill is written for.

Checked where the guarantee is kept rather than where it is made: test/README.md gives it the whole `deps:` conformance group with a row saying exactly what is asserted, and oca/README.md's opening line calls the bridge zero-dependency. The claim that it appears only in SPEC 8.5 is false.
The recommendation listed nouns rather than naming a document somebody could sit down and write.

set.recommendation: Write README.md with these sections, each answering one question: what ponder is and the problem it solves; install (install.sh and the symlink into both harnesses); the loop as one diagram; a 60-second quickstart that runs; the full command table; the convergence signals table; OCA integration and how to turn it off; where the lenses live and how to add one.

why: Every earlier finding graded a document against the code it describes. Nobody had graded the code against the documents, which is the only direction that catches a documented feature nobody built.

finding.title: `--mode build` is documented but unimplemented
finding.detail: `ponder start --mode deliberate|build` is in SPEC 5's usage line, SPEC 3.1 defines build as 'deltas may touch disk', and protocol.md:91 gives it a table row reading 'build permits deltas that touch disk'. In lib/, `session.mode` is validated at cli.js:517, stored, and read exactly once more — report.md:57 prints it. No delta path branches on it. A reader who starts a session with --mode build gets deliberate-mode behaviour and no warning.
finding.recommendation: Either mark build as reserved-and-unimplemented everywhere it appears, or have `ponder start --mode build` refuse with a message saying so. Documenting a flag that silently does nothing is worse than not offering it.

why: Both readings of the --severity wording produce identical behaviour today, so no reader is currently harmed by the ambiguity; it should not outrank findings that cost someone an afternoon.
After f-0001's recommendation was expanded into a full section list last pass, this one repeated it. Two findings issuing the same instruction is one instruction and one echo.

set.recommendation: Covered by f-0001's install section. Keep this finding only as the reason that section is load-bearing: harness-notes.md is written for an agent reasoning about its own sandbox, and a human installing the tool should not have to read it.

why: A stale test count in a prose sentence misleads nobody about how the suite behaves; ranking it alongside findings that cost a reader an afternoon inflates the apparent size of the problem.
